Each plant is placed by following Chart 3.1 (Classification of Kingdom Plantae) from the kingdom down, using the presence or absence of seeds, vascular tissues and the number of cotyledons.

| Level of the flow chart | Pea | Jowar | Fern |
|---|---|---|---|
| Kingdom | Plantae | Plantae | Plantae |
| Sub-kingdom | Phanerogamae | Phanerogamae | Cryptogamae |
| Vascular or non-vascular | Vascular plants | Vascular plants | Vascular plants |
| Division | Angiospermae | Angiospermae | Pteridophyta |
| Class | Dicotyledonae | Monocotyledonae | (Chart 3.1 ends at the division) |

- **Pea** produces seeds, so it is a **Phanerogam**. Its seeds are enclosed within the fruit (the pod), so it belongs to **Angiospermae**, and its embryo has **two cotyledons**, so it is placed in **Dicotyledonae**.
- **Jowar** (*Sorghum vulgare*) is a seed producing plant with seeds enclosed in the fruit, so it is an **Angiosperm**. Its embryo has a **single cotyledon**, it has an adventitious root system and parallel venation, so it belongs to **Monocotyledonae**.
- **Fern** (*Nephrolepis*) does not produce seeds and flowers but reproduces by spores, so it is a **Cryptogam**. It has true roots, stem and leaves with vascular tissues, so it is placed in **Pteridophyta**, the only Cryptogams with vascular tissues.
[Note: the chapter does not name pea or describe it; it is placed in Angiospermae and Dicotyledonae because its seeds are enclosed in a fruit and have two cotyledons, the characters the chapter uses for that division and class.]

| Groups of algae | Chlorophyceae | Phaeophyceae | Rhodophyceae |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Stored food | Starch (true starch) | Mannitol, laminarin and starch | Floridean starch |
| 2. Cell wall | Cellulose | Cellulose, fucans and algin | Cellulose and pectin, glued with other carbohydrates |
| 3. Major pigments | Chlorophyll a and b | Chlorophyll a, c and fucoxanthin | Chl- a, d and Phycoerythrin |

Chlorophyceae are the **green algae**, Phaeophyceae the **brown algae** and Rhodophyceae the **red algae**; algae are classified on the basis of these pigments.

| Character | Dicotyledonae | Monocotyledonae |
|---|---|---|
| Type of roots | **Tap root system** | **Adventitious root system** |
| Example | *Helianthus annuus* (sunflower), *Hibiscus rosa-sinensis* (China rose) | *Zea mays* (maize), *Sorghum vulgare* (jowar) |

| Character | Dicotyledonae | Monocotyledonae |
|---|---|---|
| Venation in the leaves | **Reticulate venation** | **Parallel venation** |
| Example | *Helianthus annuus* (sunflower), *Hibiscus rosa-sinensis* (China rose) | *Zea mays* (maize), *Sorghum vulgare* (jowar) |

| Character | Dicotyledonae | Monocotyledonae |
|---|---|---|
| Symmetry of flower | **Tetramerous or pentamerous** (floral parts in fours or fives) | Generally **trimerous** (floral parts in threes) |
| Example | *Helianthus annuus* (sunflower), *Hibiscus rosa-sinensis* (China rose) | *Zea mays* (maize), *Sorghum vulgare* (jowar) |

Many plants that grow during the monsoon complete their life cycle within that season and then die, so the land looks barren afterwards. Before dying, the **seed producing plants** (Phanerogamae) leave behind their **seeds**, and the **spore producing plants** (Cryptogamae) such as mosses and ferns leave behind their **spores**. In the next monsoon, when water is available again, these seeds and spores give rise to new plants of the same kinds, so the same varieties appear again. Water is especially important for bryophytes and pteridophytes, because bryophytes need water for fertilization and the completion of their life cycle, and both groups grow in moist, shady places; this is why plants like *Funaria* are seen in the rainy season.
[Note: the chapter does not state how seeds and spores survive the dry season until the next monsoon.]

**Phanerogamae** are the **seed producing plants**, which produce special reproductive structures that are visible. A fern does not produce seeds and flowers; it reproduces by **spores**, and its sex organs are concealed, which are the features of **Cryptogamae**. Although a fern has true roots, stem and leaves with vascular tissues, it is placed in **Pteridophyta**, the only Cryptogams with vascular tissues (vascular Cryptogams). So the presence of vascular tissue alone does not make a plant a Phanerogam; the production of seeds does.

Both *Chlamydomonas* (unicellular, microscopic, motile) and *Sargassum* (a huge macroscopic sea weed more than 60 meters long) belong to **algae** of division **Thallophyta** because they share these characters:
- The plant body is **thalloid**, i.e. undifferentiated into root, stem and leaves.
- They are mostly **aquatic** and non-vascular plants.
- They contain photosynthetic pigments including **chlorophyll**, and algae are classified on the basis of these pigments.
- The cell wall contains polysaccharides like **cellulose**, and the reserve food is starch or its other forms.
- Reproduction takes place by vegetative, asexual and sexual ways, and the life cycle shows **alternation of generation**.

Size therefore does not decide the group: *Chlamydomonas* is a green alga (Chlorophyceae) and *Sargassum* a brown alga (Phaeophyceae), but both are algae.

Maize (*Zea mays*) is a **monocot**. In Monocotyledonae the vascular bundles are conjoint, collateral and **closed**, that is, there is no **cambium** between xylem and phloem. An increase in girth comes from **secondary growth**, which needs cambium (in Dicots the cambium between xylem and phloem gives secondary growth). Since cambium is absent, secondary growth does not take place in maize, so the girth of the stem does not increase over time.
[Note: the chapter does not state in words that secondary growth is what increases the girth of a stem.]

The plant most likely belongs to **Bryophyta**, probably a **moss** such as *Funaria*. Bryophytes do not have true roots; instead they have root-like structures called **rhizoids**, which absorb water and minerals and fix the plant to the substratum. They grow in moist, shady places and need water for fertilization, so they appear in the rainy season, and mosses are among the first living beings to grow on rocks, which explains their growth on a compound wall.

The diagram shows a cell of *Spirogyra*, a multicellular, **unbranched, filamentous green alga** (Chlorophyceae), as in Fig. 3.2. Labels a correct diagram carries:
- Mucilage
- Cell wall
- Cell membrane
- Cytoplasm
- Cytoplasm strand
- Nucleus
- Chloroplast (drawn as spiral bands)
- Pyrenoid
- Vacuole

The chloroplasts carry chlorophyll a and b for photosynthesis, and the pyrenoids located on the chloroplast are associated with starch storage.

The diagram shows *Chlamydomonas*, a **unicellular, microscopic, motile green alga** (Chlorophyceae), as in Fig. 3.2. Labels a correct diagram carries:
- Chloroplast (drawn cup-shaped)
- Nucleus
- Pyrenoid (starch storage)
- Mitochondria

The figure also shows two flagella at the front end of the cell (unlabelled in the book), by which the cell is motile. The chloroplast carries chlorophyll a and b, and the stored food is true starch.

[Note: the book's Fig. 3.2 labels the mitochondria "(Amino acid synthesis)"; mitochondria are the site of cellular respiration. Standard figures of *Chlamydomonas* also show a red eyespot and contractile vacuoles near the flagella, which the book does not label.]

The diagram shows the moss *Funaria* with its gametophyte and the sporophyte borne on it, as in Fig. 3.5. Labels a correct diagram carries:
- **Sporophyte**: Capsule, Seta, foot
- **Gametophyte**: Main axis (with spirally arranged leaf-like structures), Rhizoids

The leafy gametophyte is the dominant, independent, photosynthetic phase and bears the sex organs; it is fixed in soil by multicellular branched rhizoids. The sporophyte is short lived and depends on the gametophyte for nutrition and anchorage, and its capsule produces spores.

The diagram shows the fern *Nephrolepis*, a pteridophyte, as in Fig. 3.6. Labels a correct diagram carries:
- Frond
- Blade
- Rhizome
- Roots

The figure also shows the back side and front side of a leaflet of the frond. The plant body is the dominant, independent sporophyte with true roots, an underground stem (rhizome) and large, pinnately compound leaves called **macrophylls**.

Both cycles are drawn as in Fig. 3.12 (Types of life cycle), with a haploid (n) zone above and a diploid (2n) zone below.

**Haplontic life cycle** (fungi and some algae). Labels: n and 2n zones, Haploid single-cell or multicellular organism, Mitosis (twice), Spores, Fertilization, Meiosis. Mitosis occurs only in haploid cells, and the haploid organism produces gametes by mitosis. After fertilization the zygote is the only diploid cell in the life cycle, and it undergoes meiosis.

**Haplo-diplontic life cycle** (land plants and many algae). Labels: n and 2n zones, Haploid multicellular organism, Mitosis (on both sides), Gametes, Spores, Fertilization, Meiosis, Diploid multicellular organism. Mitosis occurs in both haploid and diploid cells, so the organism has a multicellular haploid phase (the gametophyte) and a multicellular diploid phase (the sporophyte).
**Phanerogamae**, comprising **Gymnospermae** and **Angiospermae**. They produce seeds and special reproductive structures that are visible (Phaneros: visible).
**Cryptogamae**, comprising **Thallophyta**, **Bryophyta** and **Pteridophyta**. They produce spores and no seeds or flowers, and their sex organs are concealed (kryptos: hidden).
**Thallophyta** (algae). Their plant body is **thalloid**, that is, undifferentiated into root, stem and leaves, as in *Chlamydomonas*, *Spirogyra* and *Sargassum*.
**Bryophyta**. Bryophytes are mostly terrestrial but badly need water for fertilization and completion of their life cycle, so they are called **amphibious plants**.
**Pteridophyta**. Evolutionarily, pteridophytes are the first vascular and true land plants, with true roots, stem and leaves, and they are the only Cryptogams with vascular tissues.

The diagram is the alternation of generations cycle (Fig. 3.11) with its labels misplaced. The corrections are:

| Place in the diagram | Label printed | Correct label |
|---|---|---|
| Upper half (containing Sporophyte (2n)) | Gametophyte phase | **Sporophyte phase** |
| Lower half | Sporophyte phase | **Gametophyte phase** |
| Box on the right, after the sporophyte | Fertilization | **Meiosis** |
| Cells on the right, after meiosis | (unlabelled) | **Spores (1n)** |
| Bottom plant | Spores (1n) | **Gametophyte (1n)** |
| Cells on the left, before the box | Zygote (2n) | **Gametes (1n)** |
| Box on the upper left | Meiosis | **Fertilization** |
| Cell on the upper left, after the box | Gametes (1n) | **Zygote (2n)** |

The corrected sequence reads: Sporophyte (2n), Meiosis, Spores (1n), Gametophyte (1n), Gametes (1n), Fertilization, Zygote (2n), and back to Sporophyte (2n).

In my words: the life cycle of a plant has two generations, the diploid **sporophyte** and the haploid **gametophyte**. Some special diploid cells of the sporophyte divide by **meiosis** to form haploid spores, which divide mitotically to give rise to the gametophyte. The gametophyte produces male and female **gametes**, which fuse during **fertilization** to form a diploid **zygote**. The zygote divides by mitosis to form the diploid sporophyte again. Because the two generations follow one another alternately, this is called **alternation of generations**.
